title: What Codex is
plain: Codex is OpenAI's coding agent. It reads your project, edits files and runs commands to finish a task you describe. You can watch, correct and review each step.
check: You type 'fix the failing test' and press Enter. What do you expect Codex to do first, and what does it do after its first edit?
rubric: Names the steps: read the code and run the failing test to see the error, then edit the files
Says the test should run again after the edit, to check the fix
Says that while Codex works, the learner can add a note by pressing Enter in the CLI
try: Run `codex` in a small practice folder and ask: `What does this project do?` Read the answer, then type `/exit` to leave.
pitfall: Wrong belief: Codex is a chat that gives text to copy into your files. Correct: it works in your project folder, so it edits real files and runs real commands. That is why approvals and save points matter.

title: Where Codex runs
plain: Codex runs in a terminal (CLI), in an editor (IDE extension), in the ChatGPT desktop app and in the cloud. Controls and commands differ by place, so check which one you use.
check: A guide says 'type /permissions in your terminal'. You use the ChatGPT desktop app. Where do you find the same control, and why might the guide not match your screen?
rubric: Says the app has a permissions control below the composer (the message box), while the CLI uses /permissions
Says a cloud task runs in a cloud environment, not on this computer
Says a guide written for one place can show menus or commands that differ on your screen
try: Name the place you use now: terminal, IDE extension, ChatGPT desktop app or cloud. Then find its permissions setting, and do not change it yet.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a tip for one place works the same everywhere. Correct: the app and IDE extension use a control below the composer, the CLI uses /permissions, and a cloud task runs in a cloud environment built from your repository.

title: Install and sign in
plain: Codex needs an install and a sign-in. Use a ChatGPT account on a plan that includes Codex, or an API key. An API key has fewer features and bills at API rates.
check: You installed Codex, but typing `codex` in a terminal says the command is not found. What do you check first, and what do you need before you can sign in?
rubric: Opens a new PowerShell window and runs codex --version; a working install prints a version number
Checks that the install line was run in PowerShell, not in another shell, and that a new window was opened after installing
Says sign-in needs a ChatGPT account on a plan that includes Codex, or an API key
try: In a new PowerShell window, run `codex --version`. A working install prints a version number. If it says the command is not found, close the window and open a new PowerShell window.
pitfall: Wrong belief: any install line works in any terminal. Correct: the Windows line runs in PowerShell, and the macOS and Linux line uses sh, so copy only the line for your system.

title: Start in the project root
plain: Codex works from the folder where you start it. It reads AGENTS.md from the project root (the folder with .git) down to that folder, so start in the top folder.
check: Codex ignores the rules in the AGENTS.md at the top of your project, but you started it in a subfolder. What could cause this, and which two things do you check?
rubric: Says that when Codex finds no project root (a folder with .git), it checks only the folder where it started
Shows the top folder with git rev-parse --show-toplevel (or finds .git with dir) and compares it with pwd
Starts codex from the top folder that holds .git and AGENTS.md
try: In your project, run `pwd` and then `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`. Both lines should name the same folder; Git may write it with forward slashes. If Git says not a git repository, the folder has no .git yet.
pitfall: Wrong belief: any folder works, because Codex finds the project anyway. Correct: with no project root, Codex checks only the folder you start in, and starting in your home folder puts the whole home folder inside the workspace.

title: Trust a folder
plain: Codex may ask you to trust a folder. Trust lets the folder's .codex settings, rules, hooks and agents load. Until then Codex may start read-only and skip them.
check: A friend sends you a project with a .codex folder, and Codex asks whether to trust it. What could trusting switch on, and what do you read before you answer?
rubric: Says trust lets the project's .codex config, rules, hooks and agents load
Opens .codex/config.toml, .codex/rules and .codex/hooks.json (where they exist) and reads them before answering
Says a hook runs a command on this computer, so a hook needs review in /hooks before it runs
try: Before you open a downloaded project, run `dir .codex` in PowerShell. If it says the path does not exist, the project has no .codex folder.
pitfall: Wrong belief: the trust question is a formality, so Yes is always safe. Correct: Yes lets that folder's own files change how Codex runs, and hooks can run commands on your computer, so answer Yes only for folders you made or trust.

title: Approval requests
plain: An approval request appears when Codex wants to act beyond its allowed boundary, for example writing outside the project or using the network. It shows the action. You answer yes or no.
check: Codex asks approval to run a command that changes files outside your project folder. What do you check before you answer, and what would make you answer No?
rubric: Reads which command or files the request names and what it will change
Says whether the change can be undone, for example because the project is in Git or the files are copied elsewhere
Answers Yes or No on purpose and gives a reason
try: In a new practice folder, run `git init`, then start `codex` in a mode that asks first (the app label is Ask for approval; in the CLI, choose the Auto preset in /permissions) and type: Create hello.txt with the word hello, then commit it with the message Add hello. The file needs no approval; the commit does, because the sandbox keeps .git read-only. Answer No once, then run `git log`: no commit should appear.
pitfall: Wrong belief: an approval request is a formality, so a quick Yes is fine. Correct: Yes lets Codex act beyond its boundary on your computer. Read the request first, and keep a Git save point so you can go back.

title: Sandbox and approval modes
plain: The sandbox limits what Codex can touch on its own. Approvals set when it must ask. The app shows these as Ask for approval, Approve for me and Full access; the CLI uses /permissions.
check: The app shows Approve for me under the composer. What does it send to automatic review, and what stays the same?
rubric: Says eligible approval requests go to automatic review instead of the learner
Says the sandbox and the workspace boundary stay the same, because the mode changes who reviews a request, not what is allowed
Names Full access as the mode with no sandbox and no approvals, which the docs do not recommend
try: In the app, read which mode the control under the composer shows. In the CLI, type `/permissions` and read the list. Do not change anything.
pitfall: Wrong belief: Approve for me gives Codex more room to act. Correct: it keeps the same workspace boundary and only changes who answers the requests that cross it. Full access removes the sandbox, so do not use it on a personal computer.

title: Plan first with /plan
plain: Plan mode asks Codex to gather context and propose a plan before it codes. Type /plan to start it. Read the plan before you say go.
check: Codex finishes a plan and waits. What do you check before you say go, and how do you see whether any file changed while it planned?
rubric: Restates the plan's goal in the learner's own words
Runs git status or /diff to see whether any file changed, because the docs do not promise that plan mode blocks edits
Says either go, or what to change first, and gives a reason
try: In a practice Git folder, type `/plan add a file notes.txt with one sentence about cats`. Read the plan, then run `git status`.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a plan is a safe read-only step, or a promise that Codex will follow exactly. Correct: read the plan, say what to change, and check git status yourself before you approve.

title: Context window
plain: The context window is how much text Codex can use at once. It holds messages, files read and command output. When it fills, Codex can summarize older parts, so exact details can be lost.
check: After three hours in one chat, Codex stops following a rule you gave in your first message. What probably happened, and where should that rule live so it lasts?
rubric: Names a full context window, or a summary that replaced the first message, as the likely cause
Runs /status and reads the context usage line
Moves the rule into AGENTS.md, or starts a new chat with a clearer first message
try: In a chat that has run for a while, type `/status` and read the line that shows context usage. Change nothing.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a long chat remembers every word equally well, so longer is better. Correct: the window has a size limit, older details can be summarized or lost, and lasting rules belong in AGENTS.md.

title: Start a fresh chat with /clear
plain: /clear starts a fresh chat in the same CLI session. The new chat has none of the old messages. Your project files do not change.
check: You are in the middle of a project and type /clear. What is gone, what stays, and how do you look for the old chat again?
rubric: Says the chat messages are cleared while the project files stay the same
Opens /resume and looks for the old chat in the list, and says so if it is not listed
Says /clear does not undo file changes Codex already made
try: Send: Reply with only the word banana. Then type `/clear` and ask: What word did I ask you to reply with? Codex should say it does not know, because the new chat has no old messages.
pitfall: Wrong belief: /clear undoes what Codex did in the project. Correct: it only starts a new chat, so files Codex already changed stay changed. Use /diff to see the changes, and the review pane or Git to undo them.

title: Compact a long chat
plain: Compaction replaces older parts of a long chat with a short summary, which frees context. You can type /compact, or Codex can compact on its own near its token limit.
check: You told Codex in chat, 'run the tests before you say you are done.' After /compact, it stops doing that. Why does this happen, and what is the fix?
rubric: Says the summary keeps the main points, but exact instructions from early messages can be shortened or lost
Says a lasting rule belongs in AGENTS.md, which Codex reads when a session starts
Says to repeat the rule after /compact until it is written in AGENTS.md
try: In a chat that has run for a while, type `/status`, then `/compact` (confirm if asked), then `/status` again. Compare the context usage in the two readings.
pitfall: Wrong belief: compaction keeps the whole conversation in a smaller size. Correct: it keeps a summary, so exact wording and long outputs can be gone; lasting rules belong in AGENTS.md.

title: Resume a saved chat
plain: Codex saves each chat on your computer. codex resume --last reopens the newest chat from the current folder. /resume opens the list of saved chats in a running session.
check: You worked on the project on Friday. On Monday you run `codex resume --last` in another folder and Codex finds no chat. Why, and how do you get the Friday chat back?
rubric: Says --last looks only in the current folder unless --all is given
Goes to the project folder and runs codex resume --last there, or runs codex resume --all
Opens the list with codex resume or /resume and picks the chat by its name or date
try: In the project folder, run `codex resume --last`. The newest chat from this folder reopens with its earlier messages.
pitfall: Wrong belief: running `codex` again picks up my last chat. Correct: `codex` opens the interface; to return to a saved chat, use `codex resume` or `/resume`.

title: Undo a change
plain: Codex has no /rewind command. Check changes with /diff in the CLI or the review pane in the app. Undo with the app's revert, or go back to a Git save point (a commit).
check: Codex deleted notes.txt with a shell command during one turn. Which tools can bring it back, and what should you have done before that turn?
rubric: Says Codex has no /rewind, so the way back is the review pane (if Git tracks the file) or a Git save point, not a built-in undo
Says the review pane shows Git changes, so a deleted file that Git tracks can appear there and be reverted
Says to save a Git commit before a risky change, so there is a version to return to
try: Type `/diff` in the CLI, or open the review pane in the app, and read the list of changed files.
pitfall: Wrong belief: the revert action undoes everything Codex did. Correct: the review pane also shows your own uncommitted edits, so check each file before you revert it. A file Git never tracked has no saved version to return to.

title: AGENTS.md file
plain: AGENTS.md is a text file of instructions that Codex reads when a session starts. Put project facts and rules there, such as the test command. Keep each rule short and checkable.
check: Your AGENTS.md says 'be careful with files', and Codex still overwrote one. How would you rewrite that line so Codex can follow it, and how would you check that it was read?
rubric: Rewrites the line as one specific, checkable rule, for example naming the folder or file that must not change
Restarts Codex in the project folder, because AGENTS.md is read when a session starts
Asks Codex to list the instruction files it loaded, and reads the answer
try: In a practice folder (not your real project), type `/init`, read the AGENTS.md it creates, and add one rule of your own.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a rule in AGENTS.md is always obeyed, and a longer file works better. Correct: Codex reads it as guidance, not as a setting, so keep the file short and each rule checkable.

title: Memories
plain: Memories let Codex reuse context from earlier chats. They are experimental and off by default. Rules that must always apply belong in AGENTS.md.
check: You told Codex 'always use pnpm' last week, and in a new chat it still knows. Where could that knowledge come from, and how would you check whether Memories is on?
rubric: Runs /memories in the CLI, or opens Settings > Personalization in the app, and reads whether chats can use or create memories
Says local memories are stored under ~/.codex/memories on this computer, as generated files
Says a rule that must always hold belongs in AGENTS.md, because memories are only a recall helper
try: Type `/memories` in the CLI and read the current choice. Close the menu without choosing anything.
pitfall: Wrong belief: Codex remembers everything I say, so I can skip AGENTS.md. Correct: Memories are off by default, they are generated files, and they are not the only source for a rule that must always apply.
